subject: research/mimic-batch
professional: a statistician or NLP researcher who works on machine-text detection evaluation and on error control for aggregated decisions (account-level or document-set-level detection, calibration of a threshold from a finite reference sample): first checks that the threshold is set on data disjoint from the data that measures FPR, that a single random split is not read as a general effect, that the reported FPR inflation is separated from sampling noise with intervals, and whether the mean-of-scores result is more than the central limit theorem applied to a known per-text AUROC

evidence.correctness: Ran python3 batch.py from a clean tree with Python 3.13 (numpy, scipy, scikit-learn installed; 3 min CPU). results.json and results.txt came out byte-identical to the committed files (git status clean on research/mimic-batch afterwards; I had copied the originals aside first). Recomputed independently with my own script (scratchpad /tmp/claude-0/s/ind.py, loops and brute-force pair comparison, different seed 123, no split, no import of batch.py; it reuses only the mimic-threshold detector to get the news scores): news, 300 human and 300 machine texts. (1) k=1 AUROC by all 90,000 pairs = 0.969, results.txt news k=1 says 0.97. (2) k=4, p=1 AUROC 0.9999 and TPR at the 95th-percentile threshold 1.00, FPR 0.052: results.txt 1.00/1.00, FPR 0.047. (3) k=32, p=0.25 (8 machine, 24 human per batch) AUROC 0.998: results.txt 1.00. Also recomputed the README's headline table by averaging results.json over 8 families: AUROC k=1 0.935, k=2 0.979/0.876, k=4 0.997/0.941/0.805, k=8 1.000/0.982/0.878/0.732, k=16 1.000/0.998/0.944/0.805, k=32 1.000/1.000/0.985/0.822 and mean FPR 0.074, 0.069, 0.075, 0.087, 0.112, 0.150: every cell matches the README. Per-family k=32 FPR (books 0.596, poetry 0.261, wiki 0.124) matches the quoted 60/26/12%. Not checked: the detector itself (mimic-contexts/mimic-threshold, outside this subject) and the figure.
evidence.completeness: Every README feature worked end to end: 7 tests; batch.py writes results.json and results.txt for 8 families x 6 k x 4 p, cells with round(p*k)=0 skipped as stated (p=0.1 appears only from k=8, p=0.25 from k=4, p=0.5 from k=2); experiments/figure.svg exists; results reproduce. Stated 'about 2 minutes' is 3 min CPU here, minor. Next steps (SPRT, max statistic, correlated batches, adapted imitators) are listed as not done and are not claimed. No TODOs or stubs. figure.py not re-run.
evidence.verification: python3.13 -m pytest tests: 7 passed (it first failed 4 of 7 under the repo's pyenv.py environment because scipy is not part of it: the test of auroc imports scipy lazily; the README does list the pip install). Four seeded mutations in batch.py, each reverted with git checkout: (a) threshold quantile 1-target -> target: CAUGHT (test_fpr_near_target...). (b) round(p*k) -> round(p*k)+1 in mixed_means: CAUGHT by 5 tests. (c) AUROC rank formula n1(n1+1)/2 -> n1(n1-1)/2: CAUGHT (test_auroc_perfect_and_chance). (d) in simulate(), measure the false-positive rate on the calibration half instead of the held-out test half (hum = batch_means(cal,...)), which is exactly the leakage the project's headline finding is about: NOT CAUGHT, 7 passed. The tests use i.i.d. Gaussian scores whose halves are the same distribution, so a split mix-up is invisible. No test covers main(), the split itself, or the threshold-on-one-half/measure-on-the-other property, and none checks the p<1 mixed batches' AUROC value. Sound for the arithmetic helpers, blind to the design-critical step.
evidence.craft: Read batch.py (88 lines), tests/test_batch.py (50 lines), mimic-threshold/threshold.py (reused). Small, clear, vectorised, seeded and deterministic; docstrings state the design; no dead code. Defects: sys.path hack to import a sibling project's threshold.py and a lazy scipy import inside auroc() (the tests that touch it fail in an environment without scipy with a ModuleNotFoundError rather than a skip); no requirements file or pin; main() writes results with open(...).write and no context manager; a single np.random generator is shared by the calibration, test and positive draws, so changing KS or PS changes every other number (results are reproducible but not stable under a grid change); one split and seed 0 only, with no repeat over splits, which is the one thing the headline needs.
evidence.claims: Checked against files: the headline table (all 6 rows) against results.json, recomputed: backed. 'Four texts from an all-machine source reach 0.997' backed (0.997). 'Recipes at 1.00 by k=8' backed. 'Half machine needs about 8 texts for 0.98; a quarter about 32' backed (0.982, 0.985). 'FPR 7.4% at k=1, 15% at k=32; 60% books, 26% poetry, 12% wiki' backed. Mechanism claim (batch-mean spread shrinks like 1/sqrt(k) while the calibration half's error does not, so a fixed gap becomes a large FPR) is stated as the reason but not tested by any experiment: it is the correct theory, yet this run neither varies the calibration size nor repeats the split, so 'books 60%' is one random split of 150/150 that happened to differ by roughly 0.1 sigma; README does say 'one split per family' and 'no confidence intervals'. The sentence 'this extends mimic-recalib (needs about 80 calibration texts) to batches: the bigger the batch, the more calibration texts' is a conclusion the data does not directly show (no calibration-size sweep). 'Dilution costs about a factor of the machine share' is read off three shares. 'No lab affiliation' disclaimer and 'Preliminary' flag present; limitations are honest. Overall every number is backed; one inference (calibration-size scaling) is argued, not measured.
evidence.fitness: A researcher can build on it: code is small, deterministic, results are in JSON, limitations and next steps are concrete. Nearest prior work: (1) research/mimic-genshift in this repository already reports batch-mean AUROC for this same detector and suite (0.971 at k=1, 0.993 at 2, 0.999 at 4, 1.000 at 8 and 16; README line 25), so the all-machine column (0.935, 0.979, 0.997, 1.0) is a repeat on a held-out-family protocol and the README does not cite it; (2) the effect is the central limit theorem: for iid scores the AUROC of means is Phi(sqrt(k) d/sqrt 2) up to the tail shape, and for a p-machine batch the shift is p*d, which is why 'cost about a factor of p' falls out without a simulation; (3) the literature on aggregating detector scores over documents of one source and on Sadasivan et al. is cited only loosely. The genuinely new part is the calibration-noise-amplification result for the fixed-rule FPR (7% to 15% to 60% for books), but one split, no intervals and no calibration-size sweep leave it an observation. A moderator cannot use it: batches are with replacement from at most 300 texts, texts from one account are correlated, and no operational rule is proposed.
evidence.domain: A statistician would sign off on the AUROC-by-batch-mean design as a clean simulation of an iid aggregation, and would accept the correct explanation of the FPR drift (the quantile of a mean estimated from n=150 has error that does not shrink with k). They would depart on: (1) bootstrap batches from the same 150 test texts that produce the negatives and, for p<1, also the human part of the positives, so negatives and positives are not independent samples (disclosed, but it inflates AUROC at large k); (2) a single random split instead of repeated splits or a bootstrap over the calibration set, so the FPR inflation has no confidence interval although Wilson intervals already exist in mimic-threshold; (3) a plug-in empirical 95th percentile with replacement-resampled batches rather than a conformal or exact-binomial calibration, which would also solve the problem the page raises; (4) the mean statistic is not the likelihood-ratio statistic, which the page acknowledges; (5) one detector (an n-gram logistic regression on plain-prompt text), so conclusions are about the easy end of detection. Standards compared: Wald sequential testing as cited, and standard conformal calibration practice, not cited.

defects.what: Headline FPR-inflation result (7.4% at k=1 rising to 15% at k=32, books 60%) rests on one random 150/150 split per family with seed 0, no repeat, no interval, no calibration-size sweep; the 'more calibration texts needed for bigger batches' conclusion is argued, not measured

Tests cannot detect the project's central design error: measuring FPR on the calibration half instead of the held-out half passes all 7 tests (seeded mutation hum = batch_means(cal, ...) survived); tests use i.i.d. synthetic scores where the halves are identical in distribution

Novelty overstated by omission: the all-machine batch-mean AUROC column repeats numbers already reported for the same detector in mimic-genshift (0.971/0.993/0.999/1.000) and is the CLT consequence of the per-text AUROC; the README does not cite either
scipy is imported lazily inside auroc(); the repo's standard pyenv.py environment (pytest, numpy) leaves 4 of 7 tests failing with ModuleNotFoundError; no requirements file

Positives for p<1 draw their human part from the same test-half pool as the negative batches, so the two groups are not independent samples; AUROC at large k and mixed p is optimistic (disclosed in limitations, not quantified)
One shared RNG stream for calibration, test and positive draws: the numbers depend on the KS and PS grid, so adding a k changes every later cell
README says the run takes about 2 minutes; measured 3 min CPU

verdict: A small, honest, reproducible simulation: batch.py regenerates results.json and results.txt byte for byte, three numbers recomputed independently from a different seed agree to two decimals, and every cell of the README table matches the stored results. It is not at senior-professional level in verification, fitness and domain. Three of four seeded bugs were caught but the one that mattered, measuring FPR on the calibration half (the leakage the page's main finding is about), passed all tests; the interesting claim (a fixed threshold's FPR inflates as batches grow, books 60%) is one seed-0 split with no interval and no calibration-size sweep; and the positive result (a weak per-text detector becomes strong on a batch) is the CLT and was already shown for this detector in mimic-genshift without being cited. Computed against the rubric: correctness 3, claims 3, verification 2 so it does not meet the bar (verification below 3); completeness 3 so it is finished.
